3R replication script (analysis.R)

How to replicate: save the block below as analysis.R, place cleaned.csv (in the export bundle) beside it, then run Rscript analysis.R. The script prints every table shown in the app; the app's numbers were verified byte-for-byte against native R output. Package citations are in section 6.
# Reproducible analysis script generated by Telos
# Run from the folder holding cleaned.csv. Uncomment install.packages() the first time.
# install.packages(c("ggplot2"))
library(ggplot2)
d <- read.csv("cleaned.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# === 01 · Pearson correlation ===
ct <- cor.test(d[["study_hours_per_week"]], d[["exam_score"]], method = "pearson", conf.level = 0.95, alternative = "two.sided")
print(ct)
print(ggplot(d, aes(study_hours_per_week, exam_score)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm"))

4PDF report (as exported)

LaTeX source (report.tex)
\documentclass{article}

\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}

\usepackage{booktabs,graphicx,siunitx}

\begin{document}

\section{Pearson correlation}

\begin{tabular}{lllllll}
\toprule
Pair & r & 95\% CI & t & df & p & N \\
\midrule
study\_hours\_per\_week -- exam\_score & 0.41 & [0.30, 0.51] & 6.97 & 238 & $<$.001 & 240 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\includegraphics{figures/01_pearson/figure_scatter.png}

r ranges from $-$1 to +1: the sign is the direction, the magnitude the strength (\textasciitilde{}.1 small, .3 medium, .5 large). p tests whether it differs from zero; the 95\% CI shows the precision. r measures only linear association - a strong curved relationship can give r near 0, and r is sensitive to outliers, so always inspect the scatterplot (use Spearman's rs for monotonic-but-nonlinear or outlier-affected data). Correlation does not imply causation. Your significance threshold ($\alpha$) is 0.05.

study\_hours\_per\_week and exam\_score were correlated, r(238)=.41, p $<$ .001, 95\% CI [0.30, 0.51].

Statistical basis: Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (r) (Pearson, K. (1895). "Note on regression and inheritance in the case of two parents." Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 58, 240-242.); r effect-size benchmarks (.1/.3/.5) (Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Routledge.).

\end{document}

# 20 · Pearson correlation

**Question:** linear association of two numeric variables

**Scenario:** Campus study: do study hours predict exam score?

## Input configuration

- **Dataset:** `campus-study.csv`
- **Configure-data:** app defaults (auto-detected types/levels)
- **Options:** two-tailed; α 0.05; 95% CI

**Role assignments** (drag column → slot):

| Column | Role slot |
|---|---|
| `study_hours_per_week` | variable A |
| `exam_score` | variable B |
